[p. 273] **Sūrat al-Aḥzāb (The Confederates)**

Its central purpose is to urge sincerity in devoting oneself to the Creator, without seeking the approval of creatures in any way, because He is All-Knowing of what benefits them and All-Wise in what He does. He raises whom He wills, even if he is weak, and brings down whom He wills, even if he is strong. So the one who is commanded should not be concerned with hoping for the goodness of any of them or fearing their great evil and hidden deceit. The name of the surah is clear in this regard when one reflects on the story to which it alludes and which it points to. *Bismillāh*: He, whatever He wills, is *al-Raḥmān* (the Most Gracious), whose mercy spread through all existence, encompassing every being with generosity and bounty, and *al-Raḥīm* (the Most Merciful) to whoever relies upon Him, with tenderness toward him.

When the preceding surah ended with turning away from the disbelievers and awaiting what the Lord of the worlds would decide concerning them, and after establishing that the revelation of the Book comes from the One who manages this whole creation, and forbidding doubt about meeting Him, this surah opened with the command concerning the foundation of all that, and the prohibition of obeying those who oppose, whether openly or secretly, and the command to follow the revelation, the greatest of which is the Book. This is a reminder that turning away is only [a form of] obedience to God when accompanied by observance of His piety.

[p. 274] So He said: ﴿O Prophet﴾. He expressed it with the particle of intermediacy (*ayyuhā*, the vocative particle) as an indication that the time of the revelation of this surah, which was the end of the fifth year [AH], after the Battle of the Confederates, was the middle period of what came after the Hijrah, hinting that little remained of the full period of victory that the quality of prophethood, which indicates elevation, requires. He expressed it with *al-nabiyy* because the purpose of the surah requires the station of prophethood, which lies between the Lord and His servant in its nearness and elevation to His presence, when read without a hamza. If it is read with a hamza, the focus is on informing about the hidden and detailing the manifest.

Al-Hirālī said in a book of his on the principles of religion: The reality of prophethood is the arrival of a manifest unseen [matter], that is, from the Truth through revelation, to a particular one of the creation, hidden from the general people among them. Then the purpose of that arrival, which remains with that one, may be specific to his own self, and he is then a *nabī* but not a *rasūl* (messenger). It may also arrive to him, when his own affair is complete, as arrivals for establishing others, and then he becomes a *rasūl*. The first rank is very common among creation, and it is prophethood; the second is rare, so messengers are a tenth of a tenth of the prophets. Prophethood has two derivations: one of them is from *naba'* (news), which is information, and this is for one chosen from among mankind for the rank of hearing and being informed, so he is *nubbi'a* (informed) and informs others, without his having the reality of what he was informed of or what he informs of, [and so] he is not a bearer of knowledge. The second derivation is from *nubuwwah*, which means elevation and height, and this is for one who rose above the rank of news to the rank of knowledge. He was thus acquainted with the knowledge of what came to him of the unseen, in its reality and perfection. So whoever rises above the rational, descending portion to the rank of hearing is a *nabī'* with a hamza, and whoever rises above that to the rank of knowledge of its reality is a *nabī* without a hamza. Thus Ādam, peace be upon him, for example, in the knowledge of the names, is a *nabī* without a hamza, and in what lies beyond it, a *nabī'* with a hamza. [Likewise Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him, in what was shown to him of the dominion (*malakūt*), is a *nabī* without a hamza, and in what lies beyond it, a *nabī'* with a hamza.] End of quotation.

He, glorified is He, did not address him by his name, to honor his rank and elevate his station. Where He named him by his name in reports, that is for honor from another aspect, namely to identify and specify him, removing confusion about him and cutting off the doubts of the obstinate.

When He, glorified is He, addressed him with this noble name, which requires intimacy, He commanded him with fear, so He said: ﴿Fear God﴾, that is, increase in piety, O highest of creation, to the extent of your capacity, before the Lord of all majesty and honor, so that you do not turn to anything other than Him, for He is worthy of being feared because of the attributes of majesty, greatness and perfection that He has.

When He directed to him the command to fear the Beloved, the Loving Friend, He followed it with a prohibition against turning [p. 276] toward the enemy and the envier. So He said: ﴿And do not obey the disbelievers﴾, that is, those who obstruct, ﴿and the hypocrites﴾, that is, those who flatter, in any matter upon which the Creator has not sent down a command to you, even if a glimmer of fear appears or a flash of hope gleams. This applies especially to asking Us for something of what they propose, hoping for their faith, such as setting for them the time of the Hour when victory would be. They only ask that mockingly. Abū Ḥayyān said: The occasion of its revelation was that it was narrated that when the Prophet ﷺ came to Madīnah, he loved the Islam of the Jews, so some of them followed him in hypocrisy, and he would lower his side to them, and they would display advice through ways of deception, so this was revealed as a warning to him against them, and as an alert to their enmity. End of quotation.

Then He gave the reason for the command and the prohibition with what removes worries and makes one turn to them and adhere to them, so He said, hinting that they have depths in their deceit which may have been hidden from him ﷺ, and emphasizing, to encourage attention to its cause with utmost concern: ﴿Indeed, God﴾, that is, with His great perfection and the might of His majesty, ﴿is﴾ from eternity and to eternity, ﴿All-Knowing﴾, with comprehensive knowledge, ﴿All-Wise﴾, with perfect wisdom. So He does not command you with a command except that He has known what follows from it, and has perfectly ordered the setting right of the matter in it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 33, verse 1 (part 2 of 2):

Imam Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said in his *Burhan*: He (glorified is He) opened it with the command to His Prophet to be mindful of Him (*ittiqa'*), with a prohibition against inclining toward the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and with following what is revealed to him. This was to exalt his rank above the trial of those whose testing preceded, those whose mention He had put forward in the Surah of as-Sajdah, and as a command to him to submit to his Creator and to rely upon Him. ﴿And Allah speaks the truth, and He guides to the way﴾ [al-Ahzab: 4]. When what was gathered from the two surahs by way of allusion to the precedents was understood, ﴿And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance﴾ [as-Sajdah: 13], this was a basis for comforting the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) and his righteous followers. For this reason, He followed the Surah of as-Sajdah with this surah, which contains comfort and good tidings, in keeping with the known pattern of His gentleness (*lutf*) and the vastness of His mercy. So He (glorified is He) opened the surah by addressing His Prophet (ﷺ) with taqwa, and informing him of what He had already given him of the path of salvation, even though it came in the form of a command, to make him aware of the uprightness of his way and the clarity of his evidence. He addressed him with the title of Prophethood because it is a command following a warning and admonition. Although he (peace be upon him) had been exalted by Allah beyond committing anything contrary to taqwa, and was protected from everything that would conflict with the purity of his state and the loftiness of his station, nevertheless the manner of Allah's address to His servants is that whenever their mention is stripped of command and prohibition for the sake of praise (p-278), it is the place of mentioning them by their most specific and most praiseworthy attributes, as in ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him﴾ [al-Fath: 29] and the verses that follow, where he (ﷺ) is mentioned by the name of Messengership. Whenever there is a command or a prohibition, He generally shifts to the more general title. Among such instances: ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah﴾; ﴿O Prophet, urge the believers to fight﴾ [al-Anfal: 65]; ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ [at-Talaq: 1]; ﴿O Prophet, why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾ [at-Tahrim: 1]; ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [at-Tahrim: 9]; ﴿O Prophet, when believing women come to you﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 12]. This has been made clear elsewhere, and whatever comes contrary to this rule is due to a specific reason that required departing from the usual pattern, as in His saying: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67]. The reasoning here is that His saying (glorified is He) ﴿And if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67] carries a severe weight, so he was addressed by the title of Messenger, using the name of Messengership, as a kind of gentleness. This is of the same type as ﴿Allah pardon you. Why did you grant them permission?﴾ [at-Tawbah: 43]. There is some ambiguity in this. Also, when he was told "Convey" (*balligh*), this corresponded to his being mentioned as Messenger, for the one who conveys is a messenger, and a messenger is one who conveys. A Prophet is not obliged to convey unless he is sent. As for His saying: ﴿O Messenger, let not those who race to disbelief grieve you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41], its command, although a prohibition, is clearer than the first, because it is consolation for him (peace be upon him), comfort, and a command to patience and gentleness toward himself. Its category therefore returns to what comes as pure praise free of demand (p-279), and in light of what has been indicated, what comes of this kind is accounted for. Since this surah was opened with what its substance amounts to, namely informing him (peace be upon him) of this matter with the loftiness of his state and the excellence of his rank, this corresponded to what the surah contains of the category of exaltation (*tanzih*) in various places. Among them: Allah's informing us that the wives of His Prophet (ﷺ) are the mothers of the believers, so they were exalted above having the same ruling as other women, as a distinction for them and an honouring and glorifying of His Prophet (ﷺ). Among them: His saying ﴿And when the believers saw the confederates﴾ [al-Ahzab: 22], the verse, where He exalted them above any intrusion of evil or entry of doubt into their preserved beliefs and their great faith: ﴿They said, "This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us, and Allah and His Messenger have spoken the truth." And it increased them only in faith and submission﴾ [al-Ahzab: 22], and the verse after it, His saying ﴿Among the believers are men who have been true﴾ [al-Ahzab: 23], the verse. Among them: ﴿O wives of the Prophet, you are not like any other of women, if you fear Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 32], where He exalted them and clarified their nobility over all others. Among them: the exaltation and honouring of the People of the House: ﴿Allah only intends to remove from you the impurity, O People of the House﴾ [al-Ahzab: 33], the verse. Among them: the command concerning the veil: ﴿O Prophet, say to your wives and your daughters and the women of the believers that they should draw their cloaks over themselves﴾ [al-Ahzab: 59]. He exalted the believing women above the state of the Jahiliyyah of display and lack of veiling, and protected them from degradation and humiliation. Among them: His saying ﴿O you who believe, do not be like those who harmed Moses﴾ [al-Ahzab: 69]. He, exalted and high is He, enjoined them and exalted them by forbidding them from imitating those who deserved the curse and the wrath, in their bad conduct and their great offence. Besides these, the surah contains similar matters of this kind. Then He (glorified is He) followed what preceded with general good tidings and comprehensive gentleness, as in His saying (exalted is He): ﴿O Prophet, We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good tidings, and a warner﴾ [al-Ahzab: 45]; ﴿and as one who calls to Allah by His permission, and as a illuminating lamp﴾ [al-Ahzab: 46]. Then He (exalted is He) said: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers that for them is great bounty from Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 47]. And His saying (exalted is He): ﴿O you who believe, remember Allah with much remembrance﴾ [al-Ahzab: 41] up to His saying (exalted is He): ﴿a noble reward﴾ [al-Ahzab: 44]. And His saying (exalted is He): ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet. O you who believe, invoke blessings upon him and greet him with peace﴾ [al-Ahzab: 56]. And His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and the Muslim women﴾ [al-Ahzab: 35] up to His saying: ﴿and a great reward﴾ [al-Ahzab: 35]. And His saying: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and speak words of appropriate justice﴾ [al-Ahzab: 70] up to His saying: ﴿a great achievement﴾ [al-Ahzab: 71]. And His saying: ﴿And Allah will turn in forgiveness toward the believing men and believing women﴾ [al-Ahzab: 73] up to His saying: ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ahzab: 73]. And His saying (exalted is He), praising the believers for their fidelity and truthfulness: ﴿And when the believers saw the confederates, they said, "This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us, and Allah and His Messenger have spoken the truth"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 22] up to His saying: ﴿And they did not alter [their commitment] at all﴾ [al-Ahzab: 23]. And His saying (glorified is He), magnifying the sanctity of His Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers: ﴿Indeed, those who abuse Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Ahzab: 57] up to His saying: ﴿and a clear sin﴾ [al-Ahzab: 58]. In (p-281) these verses there is, for the believers, comfort, good tidings, and the magnifying of their sanctity, which breaks the force of the fear arising from the surahs of Luqman and as-Sajdah, and calms their dismay, as comfort rather than removal. Of this kind also is what the surah contains of enumerating Allah's blessings upon them and the goodness of their deliverance, as in His saying: ﴿O you who believe, remember the blessing of Allah upon you when hosts came against you, and We sent upon them﴾ [al-Ahzab: 9], up to His saying: ﴿There the believers were tested and shaken with a severe shaking﴾ [al-Ahzab: 11]. And His saying: ﴿And Allah repelled those who disbelieved in their rage; they gained no good. And Allah sufficed the believers in battle﴾ [al-Ahzab: 25], up to His saying: ﴿And Allah is over all things competent﴾ [al-Ahzab: 27]. He concluded the surah with the mention of repentance and forgiveness, the clearest witness to what was laid down as evidence of its purpose and its exposition, as made clear by "al-hamdu lillah." Since its substance is mercy, gentleness, and blessing, whose great worth cannot be measured, and whose thanks the world cannot fully render, He followed it with what is fitting of praise, namely the beginning of Surah Saba'. End.

When that was understood to imply opposition to everything an unbeliever calls to, and an unbeliever may sometimes call to some of the noble traits of character (*makarim al-akhlaq*), He restricted it with His saying: ﴿And follow﴾, that is, with the utmost of your effort.

When care for the revelation intensified here, and the one who reveals was known from many verses, His saying ﴿what is revealed﴾ was put in the passive voice. That is, it is cast down in a hidden manner, as a lover does with his beloved, ﴿to you﴾. He placed a noun in the position of a pronoun, indicating kindness in nurture (p-282), so that he would be strong in carrying out what the previous verse commanded. So He said: ﴿from your Lord﴾, that is, the One who is good to you by setting right all your affairs. Therefore, whatever He commands you, do it for your Lord, not for them, and whatever He forbids you, likewise, whether it is turning toward them, turning away from them, or anything else.

When He commanded him to follow the revelation, desiring that he do so, He gave a reason clearer than the first reason regarding the hiddenness of their plotting. So He said, mentioning the Greatest Name (*al-ism al-a'zam*) together with all the beautiful names that it indicates, as an increase in strengthening obedience, and emphasizing the encouragement as was previously mentioned, and as an indication that it is something some of the addressees find unlikely: ﴿Indeed, Allah﴾, [that is] in His greatness and perfection, ﴿is ever﴾, always, ﴿Acquainted with what you do﴾, that is, both groups' schemes, however subtle they are, ﴿well-Acquainted﴾. So do not concern yourself with their affairs, for He, glory be to Him, suffices you against them, however great they are. According to the recitation of Abu 'Amr with the third person (*bil-ghayb*), this reason becomes an exhortation to sincerity, a confirmation that He is able to set things right even when rescue seems impossible, and a negation of the trembling that may afflict souls at times of disorder.

Since the human being is the very place where the need for emphasizing reliance arises, He said: ﴿And put your trust﴾, meaning: leave off relying on your own management in your affairs, and rely in them ﴿upon Allah﴾, the One whose knowledge and power encompass all things. As for the repetition of this name, the [Greatest] one that comprises all the meanings of the Names in this context, it has a significance that is not hidden, as has been pointed out.

Since the implied meaning is: "Indeed, He suffices you in all of that," he followed it with His saying: ﴿And sufficient is Allah﴾, meaning the One to whom belongs all the command absolutely, ﴿as Disposer of affairs﴾, meaning: there is none more sufficient than Him for everyone who entrusts to Him his affairs. So do not turn, in any matter of yours, to anything [other than Him], for you do not have two hearts with which you turn each of them [toward one].

ولَمّا كانَ النّازِعُ إلى جِهَتَيْنِ [i.e., the one inclined toward two directions] والمُعالِجُ لِأمْرَيْنِ مُتَبايِنَيْنِ كَأنَّهُ يَتَصَرَّفُ بِقَلْبَيْنِ، أكَّدَ أمْرَ الإخْلاصِ في جَعْلِ الهَمِّ هَمًّا واحِدًا فِيما يَكُونُ مِن أُمُورِ الدِّينِ والدُّنْيا، وفي المُظاهَرَةِ والتَّبَنِّي وكُلِّ ما شابَهَها بِضَرْبِ المَثَلِ بِالقَلْبَيْنِ - كَما قالَ الزُّهْرِيُّ (al-Zuhri), فَقالَ مُعَلِّلًا لِما قَبْلَهُ بِما فِيهِ مِنَ الإشارَةِ إلى أنَّ الآدَمِيَّ مَعَ قَطْعِ النَّظَرِ عَنْ رُتْبَةِ النُّبُوَّةِ مَوْضِعٌ لِخَفاءِ الأُمُورِ عَلَيْهِ: ﴿ما جَعَلَ اللَّهُ﴾ أيِ الَّذِي لَهُ الحِكْمَةُ البالِغَةُ، والعَظَمَةُ الباهِرَةُ، ولَيْسَ الجَعْلُ إلّا لَهُ ولا أمْرَ لِغَيْرِهِ ﴿لِرَجُلٍ﴾ أيْ لِأحَدٍ مِن بَنِي آدَمَ الَّذِينَ هم أشْرَفُ الخَلائِقِ مِن نَبِيٍّ ولا غَيْرِهِ، وعَبَّرَ بِالرَّجُلِ لِأنَّهُ أقْوى جِسْمًا وفَهْمًا فَيُفْهِمُ غَيْرَهُ مِن بابِ الأوْلى؛ وأشارَ إلى التَّأْكِيدِ (p-٢٨٤) بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿مِن قَلْبَيْنِ﴾ وأكَّدَ الحَقِيقَةَ وقَرَّرَها، وجَلّاها وصَوَّرَها لِما قَدْ يَظُنُّ الإنْسانُ مِن أنَّهُ يَقْدِرُ عَلى صَرْفِ النَّفْسِ إلى الأُمُورِ المُتَخالِفَةِ كَما يَفْعَلُ المُنافِقُ، بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿فِي جَوْفِهِ﴾ أيْ حَتّى يَتَمَكَّنَ مِن أنْ يَنْزِعَ بِكُلِّ قَلْبٍ إلى جِهَةٍ غَيْرِ الجِهَةِ الَّتِي نَزَعَ إلَيْها القَلْبُ الآخَرُ، لِأنَّ ذَلِكَ مُودٍ إلى خَرابِ البَدَنِ، لِأنَّ القَلْبَ مُدَبِّرُهُ بِإذْنِ اللَّهِ تَعالى، واسْتِقْلالُ كُلٍّ بِالتَّدْبِيرِ يُؤَدِّي إلى الفَسادِ كَما مَضى في دَلِيلِ التَّمانُعِ سَواءٌ؛ قالَ الرّازِي (al-Razi) في اللَّوامِعِ (al-Lawami'): القَلْبُ كالمِرْآةِ مَهْما حُوذِيَ بِهِ جانِبُ القُدْسِ أعْرَضَ عَنْ جانِبِ الحِسِّ، ومَهْما حُوذِيَ بِهِ جانِبُ الحِسِّ أعْرَضَ عَنْ جانِبِ القُدْسِ، فَلا يَجْتَمِعُ الإقْبالُ عَلى اللَّهِ وعَلى ما سِواهُ. انْتَهى. وحاصِلُ ذَلِكَ أنَّهُ تَمْهِيدٌ لِأنَّ التَّوَزُّعَ والشِّرْكَ لا خَيْرَ فِيهِ، وأنَّ مُدَبِّرَ المُلْكِ واحِدٌ كَما أنَّ البَدَنَ قَلْبٌ واحِدٌ، فَلا التِفافَ إلى غَيْرِهِ، وأنَّ الدِّينَ لَيْسَ بِالتَّشَهِّي وجَعْلِ الجاعِلِينَ، وإنَّما هو بِجَعْلِهِ سُبْحانَهُ، فَإنَّهُ العالِمُ بِالأُمُورِ عَلى ما هي عَلَيْهِ.

ولَمّا كانَ كُلٌّ مِنَ المُظاهَرَةِ والتَّبَنِّي نازِعًا إلى جِهَتَيْنِ مُتَنافِيَتَيْنِ، وكانَ أهْلُ الجاهِلِيَّةِ يَعُدُّونَ الظِّهارَ (ẓihār, a pre-Islamic form of divorce in which a husband declared his wife to be like his mother's back) طَلاقًا مُؤَبَّدًا لا رَجْعَةَ فِيهِ - كَما نَقَلَهُ ابْنُ المُلَقِّنِ (Ibn al-Mulaqqin) في عُمْدَةِ المِنهاجِ (ʿUmdat al-Minhaj) عَنْ صاحِبِ الحاوِي (al-Hawi), وكانَ المُخاطَبُونَ قَدْ أعْلاهُمُ الوَعْظُ السّابِقُ إلى التَّأهُّلِ لِلْخِطابِ، لَفَتَ سُبْحانَهُ القَوْلَ إلَيْهِ عَلى قِراءَةِ الغَيْبِ [فِي ”يَعْلَمُونَ“ لِأبِي عَمْرٍو] فَقالَ: ﴿وما جَعَلَ أزْواجَكُمُ﴾ (p-٢٨٥) أيْ بِما أباحَ لَكم مِنَ الِاسْتِمْتاعِ بِهِنَّ مِن جِهَةِ الزَّوْجِيَّةِ؛ ثُمَّ أشارَ إلى الجِهَةِ الأُخْرى بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿اللائِي تُظاهِرُونَ مِنهُنَّ﴾ أيْ [كَما] يَقُولُ الإنْسانُ لِلْواحِدَةِ مِنهُنَّ: أنْتِ عَلَيَّ كَظَهْرِ أُمِّي ﴿أُمَّهاتِكُمْ﴾ بِما حَرُمَ عَلَيْكم مِنَ الِاسْتِمْتاعِ بِهِنَّ حَتّى تَجْعَلُوا ذَلِكَ عَلى التَّأْبِيدِ وتُرَتِّبُوا عَلى ذَلِكَ أحْكامَ الأُمَّهاتِ كُلَّها، لِأنَّهُ لا يَكُونُ لِرَجُلٍ أمانٌ، ولَوْ جَعَلَ ذَلِكَ لَضاقَ الأمْرُ، واتَّسَعَ الخَرْقُ، وامْتَنَعَ الرَّتْقُ ﴿وما جَعَلَ أدْعِياءَكُمْ﴾ بِما جَعَلَ لَهم مِنَ النِّسْبَةِ والِانْتِسابِ إلى غَيْرِكم ﴿أبْناءَكُمْ﴾ بِما جَعَلْتُمْ لَهم مِنَ الِانْتِسابِ إلَيْكم لِيَحِلَّ لَهم إرْثُكُمْ، وتَحْرُمَ عَلَيْكم حَلائِلُهم وغَيْرُ ذَلِكَ مِن أحْكامِ الأبْناءِ، ولا يَكُونُ لِابْنٍ أبَوانِ، ولَوْ جُعِلَ ذَلِكَ لَضاعَتِ الأنْسابُ، وعَمَّ الِارْتِيابُ، وانْقَلَبَ كَثِيرٌ مِنَ الحَقائِقِ أيَّ انْقِلابٍ، فانْفَتَحَ بِذَلِكَ مِنَ الفَسادِ أبْوابٌ أيُّ أبْوابٍ، فَلَيْسَ زَيْدُ بْنُ حارِثَةَ بْنِ شَراحِيلَ الكَلْبِيُّ الَّذِي تَبَنَّيْتَهُ ابْنًا لَكَ أيُّها النَّبِيُّ بِتَبَنِّيكَ لَهُ جَزاءً [لَهُ] بِاخْتِيارِهِ لَكَ عَلى أبِيهِ وأهْلِهِ، وهَذا تَوْطِئَةٌ لِما يَأْتِي مِن قِصَّةِ زَواجِ النَّبِيِّ ﷺ لِزَيْنَبَ بِنْتِ جَحْشٍ مُطَلَّقَةِ زَيْدٍ مَوْلى رَسُولِ اللَّهِ (p-٢٨٦) ﷺ [فَإنَّهُ ﷺ] لَمّا تَزَوَّجَها قالَ المُنافِقُونَ كَما حَكاهُ البَغَوِيُّ (al-Baghawi) وغَيْرُهُ: تَزَوَّجَ مُحَمَّدٌ امْرَأةَ ابْنِهِ وهو يَنْهى النّاسَ عَنْ ذَلِكَ، فَأنْزَلَ اللَّهُ هَذِهِ الآيَةَ، وبَيَّنَ أنَّ التَّبَنِّيَ إنَّما هو مَجازٌ، وأنَّ المُحَرَّمَ إنَّما هو زَوْجَةُ الِابْنِ الحَقِيقِيِّ [و] ما أُلْحِقَ بِهِ مِنَ الرَّضاعِ، وذَلِكَ أنَّ النَّبِيَّ ﷺ كانَ تَبَنّى زَيْدًا لِقِصَّةٍ مَذْكُورَةٍ في السِّيرَةِ، رَوى البُخارِيُّ عَنِ ابْنِ عُمَرَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُما أنَّ زَيْدَ بْنَ حارِثَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ مَوْلى رَسُولِ اللَّهِ ﷺ ما كُنّا نَدْعُوهُ إلّا زَيْدَ بْنَ مُحَمَّدٍ حَتّى نَزَلَ القُرْآنُ ﴿ادْعُوهم لآبائِهِمْ﴾ [الأحزاب: ٥].

لَمّا أبْطَلَ [هَذا] سُبْحانَهُ، اسْتَأْنَفَ الإخْبارَ عَمّا مَضى مِن عَمَلِهِمْ فِيهِ فَقالَ: ﴿ذَلِكُمْ﴾ أيِ القَوْلُ البَعِيدُ عَنِ الحَقِيقَةِ، وأكَّدَ هَذا بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿قَوْلُكم بِأفْواهِكُمْ﴾ أيْ لا حَقِيقَةَ لَهُ وراءَ القَوْلِ وتَحْرِيكِ الفَمِ [مِن غَيْرِ مُطابَقَةِ قُلُوبِكُمْ،] فَإنَّ كُلَّ مَن يَقُولُ ذَلِكَ لا يَعْتَقِدُهُ، [لِأنَّ مَن كانَ لَهُ فَمٌ كانَ مُحْتاجًا، ومَن كانَ مُحْتاجًا كانَ مُعَرَّضًا لِلنَّقائِصِ كانَ مُعَرَّضًا لِلْأوْهامِ، ومَن غَلَبَتْ عَلَيْهِ الأوْهامُ كانَ في كَلامِهِ الباطِلُ] ﴿واللَّهُ﴾ أيِ المُحِيطُ عِلْمُهُ وقُدْرَتُهُ [ولَهُ جَمِيعُ صِفاتِ الكَمالِ] ﴿يَقُولُ الحَقَّ﴾ أيِ الكامِلَ (p-٢٨٧) فِي حَقِّيَّتِهِ، الثّابِتَ الَّذِي يُوافِقُ ظاهِرُهُ باطِنَهُ، فَلا قُدْرَةَ لِأحَدٍ عَلى نَقْضِهِ، فَإنْ أخْبَرَ عَنْ شَيْءٍ فَهو كَما قالَ، لَيْسَ بَيْنَ الخَبَرِ والواقِعِ مِن ذَلِكَ المُخْبَرِ عَنْهُ شَيْءٌ مِنَ المُخالَفَةِ، وإنْ أتى بِقِياسِ فَرْعٍ عَلى أصْلٍ لَمْ يَسْتَطِعْ أحَدٌ إبْداءَ فَرْقٍ، [فَإنَّ أقْوالَهُ سُبْحانَهُ سابِقَةٌ عَلى الواقِعِ لِأنَّها مُصَدَّرَةٌ فِيها بِكَوْنٍ، فَإذا قالَ قَوْلًا وُجِدَ مَضْمُونُهُ مُطابِقًا لِذَلِكَ القَوْلِ، فَإذا طَبَّقْتَ بَيْنَهُما كانا سَواءً، فَكانَ ذَلِكَ المَضْمُونُ ثابِتًا كَما كانَ ذَلِكَ الواقِعُ ثابِتًا، فَكانَ حَقًّا، هَكَذا أقْوالُهُ عَلى الدَّوامِ، لِأنَّهُ مُنَزَّهٌ سُبْحانَهُ عَنِ النَّقائِصِ فَلا جارِحَةَ ثَمَّ لِيَكُونَ بَيْنَها وبَيْنَ مُعَدِّ القَوْلِ مُخالَفَةٌ مِن فَمٍ أوْ غَيْرِهِ وعَنْ كُلِّ ما يَقْتَضِي حاجَةً، فالآيَةُ مِنَ الِاحْتِباكِ (ihtibak, a rhetorical device in which two contrasting elements are mentioned and each is omitted where the other is stated): ذَكَرَ الفَمَ أوَّلًا دَلِيلًا عَلى نَفْيِهِ ثانِيًا، والحَقَّ ثانِيًا دَلِيلًا عَلى ضِدِّهِ الباطِلِ أوَّلًا، وسِرُّ ذَلِكَ أنَّهُ ذَكَرَ ما يَدُلُّ عَلى النَّقْصِ في حَقِّنا، وعَلى الكَمالِ في حَقِّهِ، ودَلَّ عَلى التَّنْزِيهِ بِالإشارَةِ لِيُبَيِّنَ فَهْمَ الفُهَماءِ وعِلْمَ العُلَماءِ] ﴿وهُوَ﴾ أيْ وحْدَهُ مِن حَيْثُ قَوْلُهُ الحَقُّ ﴿يَهْدِي السَّبِيلَ﴾ أيِ الكامِلَ الَّذِي مِن شَأْنِهِ أنْ يُوصِلَ إلى المَطْلُوبِ، إنْ ضَلَّ أحَدٌ في فِعْلٍ أوْ قَوْلٍ، فَلا تُعَوِّلُوا عَلى سَواهُ ولا تَلْتَفِتُوا أصْلًا إلى غَيْرِهِ.

Since it was as if it were said, "What then do you say? Guide us to the path of truth in this matter," He directed to the matter of adoption, indicating that it is the principal aim of this surah, because of the effects that come after it, which are the intended ones in themselves, by His saying: ﴿Call them﴾, that is, the adopted sons, (p-288) ﴿by their fathers' names﴾, that is, if they know a son's father they say: "Zayd ibn Harithah." Then He gave the reason for this by His saying: ﴿That is﴾, that is, this calling, ﴿more just﴾, that is, closer to justice than adoption, although adoption was only for greater compassion toward the adopted son and kindness to him, ﴿in the sight of Allah﴾, that is, the One who combines all attributes of perfection, so nothing should be done in His dominion except what is closest to perfection. In this there is, in relation to what came before, some relief for them, and an indication that that severity was in relation to the totality of the two previous statements.

Since they might be unknown, His saying ﴿But if you do not know their fathers﴾, whether from original or subsequent ignorance, is made to follow from this, ﴿then they are your brothers in religion﴾, if they had entered your religion, ﴿and your clients﴾, that is, your slaves while slavery continues, or freed slaves, in both states. For this reason they said: "Salim, client of Abu Hudhayfah." When this was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever claims a lineage other than his father's while knowing it, Paradise is forbidden to him." Related by al-Shaykhan from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Abu Bakrah, may Allah be pleased with them both.

Since their custom was to fear what had preceded from their conditions regarding the prohibition, because of the intensity of their scrupulousness, He informed them that He, exalted is He, had removed that from them because it was an error, and He framed it in a manner that covers what comes after the prohibition [also], so He said: ﴿And there is no blame upon you﴾, that is, (p-289) sin, inclination, or deviation, and He expressed it with the adverbial form (fi) so as to repeat that an error has no sin in it in any way; had He expressed it with (bi) one might have thought there was sin in it, but He pardoned it, so He said: ﴿in what you have erred in﴾, that is, of calling (them) by sonship and of backing, or in something before the prohibition or after it. His saying ﴿but what your hearts intend﴾, that is, the sin lies in what your hearts intend, indicates the removal of blame also for what occurred after the prohibition through forgetfulness or slip of the tongue. The feminine form of the verb indicates that no one adopts it after clear explanation except a heart in which there is the softness of femininity, and the plural of abundance indicates the generality of sin if one who intends it is not forbidden.

Since this generosity was specific to what preceded it, He, glorified is He, generalized by His saying: ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾, that is, because He is not greater than Him nor more generous than Him, ﴿Forgiving﴾, that is, among His attributes is thorough concealment of the sinner who repents, ﴿Merciful﴾, the great guidance of the strayed who returns, and honoring by granting what is desired.

When the Exalted (subḥānahu) had forbidden adoption (tabannī), and the Prophet ﷺ had adopted Zayd ibn Ḥārithah, his freed slave, because he had chosen him over his own father and mother, He (subḥānahu) gave the reason for the prohibition in this particular case by His saying, indicating that the matter is greater than that: ﴿The Prophet﴾, that is, the one whom Allah informs of the subtle details of circumstances in the wondrous words, and whom He always elevates to the stations of perfection, and does not wish to occupy him with a child or wealth. ﴿Is closer to the believers﴾, that is, those firmly rooted in faith; so others are closer in every matter of the affairs of religion (p-290) and the world, because of what he has attained of the Lordly presence. ﴿Than their own selves﴾, let alone their fathers, in the enforcement of his judgment over them and the obligation of obedience to him, because he calls them only to reason and wisdom, and commands them only with what saves them, whereas their selves call them only to desire and temptation, and so command them with what destroys them. Thus he manages them with the management of fathers, rather, of kings [rather] greater than that, by this Lordly means, so what need has he for a bodily means? ﴿And his wives﴾, that is, those with whom he has consummated marriage, because of the sanctity they have due to him, ﴿are their mothers﴾, that is, the mothers of the believing men specifically, not of the women, because there is no danger from the side of women; this applies in sanctity, honor, veneration and respect, and the prohibition of marriage, but not in permissibility of seclusion, looking, and other rulings; and there is no veneration between them and the mothers in this at all. Therefore it is not lawful to violate their sanctity in any way, nor to approach their presence with any kind of deficiency, because the right of the Prophet ﷺ over his community is greater than the right of a parent over his child, and he is alive in his grave. This is a matter Allah has decreed, and when He decrees something it occurs, for the command is His command and the creation is His creation, and He is the Knower of what benefits them and what harms them: ﴿Does not He who created know? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾ [al-Mulk: 14]. Al-Shaykhān narrated from Abū Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him (p-291), from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "There is no believer except that I am the closest of people to him in this world and the Hereafter. Recite, if you wish: ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves﴾. So whichever believer leaves wealth, let his heirs—whoever they are—inherit it; and if he leaves debt or dependents, let him come to me, for I am his guardian."

When Allah (subḥānahu) returned things to their origins and forbade dispersion and division, and among that was the matter of adoption, and among what branches from it is inheritance, according to what was formerly the case of migration, support and the brotherhood which the Prophet ﷺ established when the matter needed it, and that was abrogated by the verse at the end of al-Anfāl, which precedes this surah in arrangement and in revelation, and what is mentioned here was a single instance entering within the generality of the expression in that verse, He repeated it here for emphasis and explicit specification of this instance, out of concern for it, along with what it contains of detail and addition, so He said: ﴿And those of blood-relationship﴾, that is, relatives by kinds of kinship, including prophethood and other things, ﴿are closer﴾ by the right of kinship ﴿to one another﴾ in all general benefits: for the call, inheritance, support and connection. ﴿In the Book of Allah﴾, that is, in the decree of Him to whom all command belongs, and there is no command for anyone with Him, and His judgment is as was previously stated in this Book of yours, and as the hadith mentioned just above has indicated (p-292).

When He had explained that they are closer by reason of kinship, He explained what they are preferred over, saying: ﴿than﴾, that is, they are closer by reason of kinship than ﴿the believers﴾, the Helpers, without a preferential kinship, ﴿and the emigrants﴾, the believers without such kinship likewise. Since the meaning is "closer in every benefit," He made an exception from it according to the rule of excepting from the most general, by His saying, turning the arrangement toward the style of address so that the addressees may understand that they are characterized by firmness in faith, which was indicated in the verse of priority by the expression of description, and this urges them to do what is good: ﴿except that you do﴾ [that is], while you are conveying and directing ﴿to your allies﴾ by slavery, or adoption, or alliance, in health absolutely and in illness from the third, as a bequest or by way of a bequest ﴿a kindness﴾ by which you benefit them. In that case that ally becomes entitled to it, and a blood-relative is not closer than him; rather, there is no bequest to an heir.

When He had informed that this ruling is in the Book of Allah, He repeated the admonition about it as emphasis, uprooting this ruling which was fixed in minds by His establishing it previously, so He said, resuming: ﴿That was﴾ [that is], this great decree ﴿in the Book﴾ (p-293), that is, the Qur'an, at the end of the chapter of al-Anfāl, ﴿inscribed﴾ by an expression that encompasses it. Al-Iṣbahānī said: It has also been said: in the Torah, because in the Torah: when a man arrives among people of his religion, they must honor him and console him, and his inheritance goes to his close relatives. The verse is of the type of iḥtibāk (interlocking omission): it mentioned the attribute of faith first as an indication of its omission second, and it mentioned the attribute of migration second as an indication of the omission of support first.

When changing customs and altering familiar practices is very hard on people, and separates those who are gathered together, cuts off those who are connected, and drives apart those who are close, he said, reminding him (ﷺ) of what was taken from those before him: that their religions would be abrogated (naskh) by his religion, that their familiar practices would be changed by his familiar practice, and that they would advise their peoples by delivering to them everything they were sent with. He turned the speech to the manifestation of greatness, because that is more conducive to the acceptance of commands: ﴿And when﴾. So it is understood that the implied meaning is: "Remember that," that is, what We have written for you [in your Book] before this, and remember when ﴿We took﴾, by Our greatness, ﴿from the prophets their covenant﴾ to convey the message in ease and in hardship, to confirm one another, and to follow you in what We informed you of in Our saying: ﴿When I gave you a Book and wisdom, and then there came to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and help him﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 81], and their saying: "We affirm."

When He reminded him of the covenant taken from all the prophets concerning the alteration of their familiar practices to what the Exalted commanded them, namely conveying what was revealed to them and acting upon its requirements (p-294), He reminded him of the covenant taken from him concerning conveyance, and said: ﴿And from you﴾, that is, in Our saying in this surah: ﴿Fear Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 1] ﴿and follow what is revealed to you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 2], and in al-Ma'idah: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message; and Allah will protect you from the people﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67]. So do not concern yourself with considering an enemy or a close friend, whether insignificant or great.

When he had completed the intended meaning in general and comprehensive terms, and singled out the Prophet (ﷺ) from that generality, beginning with him to show his honor, and because he is the one directly intended by the command to piety and to following revelation, for the sake of adoption and other matters, He followed him with the rest of the Ulu al-'Azm (the prophets of firm resolve), who are the possessors of Books and the renowned masters of sacred laws, to emphasize the matter and magnify the station. For whoever is known to have a share in a matter strives to precede others in it; and He arranged them according to their chronological order, since He did not intend to rank them above one another, but rather to give consolation through the earlier and the later ones. So He said: ﴿And from Noah﴾, the first of the messengers sent to those who opposed them, ﴿and Abraham﴾, father of the prophets, ﴿and Moses﴾, the first of the possessors of Books among the prophets of the Children of Israel, ﴿and Jesus, son of Mary﴾, the last of them. He ascribed him to his mother as a call against those who went astray concerning him, by way of rebuke and recording the disgrace. Then He increased the emphasis and magnification of the matter, magnifying the covenant itself, and indicating its hardship, so He said, emphasizing by repeating the verb and by the manifestation of greatness, because returning from what is familiar is difficult: ﴿And We took from them﴾, that is, by Our greatness in that, ﴿a firm covenant﴾, a metaphor (isti'arah) borrowed from describing massive bodies, and a metonymy (kinayah) for the fact that it cannot be severed by anyone who wishes to be connected to Us.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 33, verse 8:

When the taking of the covenant from the Prophets was a taking of it from their communities as well, and disbelief is punished without any condition, while obedience is rewarded only on the condition of sincerity (ikhlas), He gave the reason for this, expressing it in terms of the central theme of the surah. He said, turning to the third-person mode (maqam al-ghaybah) in order to magnify the awe, because when address (al-khitab) is prolonged the addressee becomes familiar and at ease: ﴿That He may ask﴾, i.e. on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿the truthful ones﴾, i.e. in fulfilling the covenant, ﴿about their truthfulness﴾, whether it was for God alone, sincerely, or not, as an honouring of them, a humiliation and a rebuke to the liars. He will also ask the disbelievers about their disbelief, what it was that moved them to it, while the situation is that He has prepared a great reward for the truthful. ﴿And He has prepared for the disbelievers﴾, i.e. those who conceal (al-satirin) the radiance of the lights of the covenant, ﴿a painful punishment﴾. So the verse is one of the finest examples of riyad al-ihtibak (the mutual implication of opposites), and he only explicitly mentioned the questioning of the truthful as glad tidings to them of their honour in that great station, and he omitted the questioning of the disbelievers to indicate their contempt for the disgrace of lying: ﴿And they swear falsely about God while they know﴾ [al-Mujadila: 14], ﴿They swear to Him as they swear to you﴾ [al-Mujadila: 18], and he mentioned what is more painful to them.

[p. 296] When He, glory be to Him, had emphasized the obligation to proclaim all of His command, even if the hardship was great and its anguish increased, without inclining toward any agreeable companion, and without concern for any opponent who opposes, relying on His management and the greatness of His affair in His decree, He reminded them with an observed proof, which is the greatest of their battles and the most severe of the distresses that befell them. He said, making known that what is intended in essence by the commands that preceded is the Community. He directed the command to the Imam so that it would be more compelling to them to comply. The command given to the Prophet ﷺ is existential (takwini), like what God Most High says to him, "Be," so the reality is will, not command. The command addressed to those who believe is obligatory (takfili, charging a duty). Something may be intended from them that they are commanded to do, and it may not be intended. The command addressed to people is argumentative (ihtijaji), meaning that the proof is established against them by it. It is verified that some of them are intended to do the opposite of what they were commanded: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, meaning, those who professed belief. He expressed it this way so that it would include the hypocrites. ﴿Remember﴾ and He encouraged them to give thanks by mentioning the favor and by explicitly naming the Greatest Name, so He said: ﴿the favor of Allah﴾. He expressed it this way because it is the favor intended in essence, and what is meant is the bestowal of the Supreme King, for whom there is no equal, ﴿upon you﴾, meaning, so that you would thank Him for it by complying with His command without turning to the opposition of anyone, whoever he may be, for indeed Allah is sufficient for you against everything you fear. Then He mentioned to them the time of that favor, as an elaboration of its depiction, so that He might remind them of what they were in during it, and He said: ﴿when﴾, meaning, at the time when ﴿there came upon you﴾ [meaning] in the battle of the Trench, [p. 297] when the confederates gathered against you. The Prophet ﷺ had dug the trench when he heard of them, on the advice of Salman al-Farisi, may Allah be pleased with him, along the two sides of Sala' on its north. He marked it out and allotted to every ten men forty cubits. They were three thousand, so the trench was twelve thousand cubits. ﴿Hosts﴾, and they were the confederates from Quraysh and those who joined them from the Ahabish, four thousand strong, led by Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, and those from the tribes of the Arabs who joined them: from Banu Sulaym, led by Abu al-A'war; from Banu 'Amir, led by 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl; from Ghatafan, led by 'Uyayna ibn Hisn; from Banu Asad, led by Tulayha ibn Khuwaylid; and from the tribes of the Children of Israel among the Jews, and from Banu al-Nadir and their chiefs, Huyayy ibn Akhtab and the two sons of Abu al-Huqayq. They are the ones who gathered the confederates because of the Prophet's ﷺ expulsion of Banu al-Nadir from the noble city of Madina. They also corrupted Banu Qurayza, who were in the noble city, and their leader was Ka'b ibn Asad. The total was twelve thousand. They were confident in their assumption that they would not turn back, while some remnant of Islam remained, and none of its people would have any protection.

When the coming of the hosts was terrifying, He consequently returned to the manifestation of greatness and said: ﴿So We sent﴾, meaning, as a result of that, when We saw your inability to face them and to resist them in fighting, We inspired you to dig the trench so that it would prevent them from easily reaching you. Then, when their stay was prolonged, We sent, with the greatness We possess, ﴿against them﴾, meaning, specifically, ﴿a wind﴾, which was the east wind (al-Saba), and it extinguished their fires, [p. 298] overturned their cooking pots and their large bowls, threw dust into their faces, pelted them with stones, demolished their tents, weakened their bones with its cold, and dispersed their horses. And ﴿hosts you did not see﴾. It is valid for the seeing to be visual or of the heart. Among them, from humans, was Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud al-Ghatafani, may Allah be pleased with him, whom Allah guided to Islam. He came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "No one knows of my Islam, so command me, O Messenger of Allah, with your order!" He said: "You are among us a single man, and war is deception, so cause discord among them as much as you can." He set the Jews and the Arabs against each other by telling the Jews, who were his allies: "These people, meaning the Arabs, if they see an opportunity they will seize it, and otherwise they will withdraw to their lands returning. But your situation is not like theirs. The land is your land, and your wealth, your women, and your children are in it. So do not fight with them until you take from them a pledge from their nobles, to remain with you until you finish off the man, for you have no strength left against him if he is alone with you." They said: "You have advised well." He said: "Keep this secret from me." Then he said to Quraysh: "You know my companionship with you and my separation from Muhammad, and I have heard a matter that I do not think you would accuse me of." They said: "You are not accused by us." He said: "Keep it secret from me." They said: "We will." He said: "The Jews [p. 299] have regretted breaking what was between them and Muhammad, and they sent to him: 'We have repented; would it benefit us with you if we took for you a group of the people's nobles, whose necks you strike, and we will be with you against the rest, until you are finished with them, so that you stop against us and restore our security?'" He said: "Yes. But if they send to you, do not hand over a single man to them." Then he went to Ghatafan and said: "You are my origin and my clan, and the people most beloved to me." They said: "You have spoken truly." Then he told them the same as he had told Quraysh and asked them to keep it secret. Then Qurayza sent to them, asking them for a pledge. They said: "Nu'aym has spoken truly," and they refused to hand over anyone to them. Qurayza said: "Nu'aym has spoken truly." So they abandoned one another, their word was divided, their strength was broken, and their vigor cooled.

Among them, from the angels, was Jibril, peace be upon him, and whoever Allah willed from them, upon all of them the best of blessings and peace, and greetings and honor. They shouted Allahu Akbar in the corners of their camp, shook them, and spread terror into their hearts. Their horses trembled, and their talk and their saying came to nothing. So that was their departure, after about forty days or twenty-some, according to what was said.

When He, glory be to Him, had summarized the story despite its length in part of this verse, He detailed it. He said, mentioning the Greatest Name, as an indication that what occurred in it was a matter given attention, [p. 300] with the utmost effort, although for Him, glory be to Him, all of it is easy: ﴿And Allah is ever﴾, Who possesses all attributes of perfection, majesty, and beauty, ﴿of what you do﴾, meaning, the confederates' scheming, gathering, combining, plotting, deception, and evil intent, according to the reading of al-Basri, and you, O Muslims, who dug the trench and [did] other things out of sincerity in faith [and other than that], according to the reading of the rest. ﴿Seeing﴾, possessing complete sight and knowledge. So He arranged in this war what made the Muslims the superior ones. Their strength did not benefit the people of polytheism, their multitude did not avail them, and the Believers' fewness did not harm them. We made that a cause of their enrichment with the wealth of Banu Qurayza, their women and children, and a cure for their ailments through the shedding of their blood, as will come later.

Then He reminded them of the severe ordeal that befell them through their confederacy, saying, in apposition to the first ﴿when﴾: ﴿When they came upon you﴾, meaning the aforementioned armies, beginning with those nearest to them, because the nearest is the best at spotting weakness and the best informed about harm.

Since it was known that they did not surround everything above and below, He introduced the partitive particle, saying: ﴿from above you﴾, meaning the Banu Qurayzah, Asad and Ghatafan, from the direction of the outflow of the torrents, from the east. He added "above" to their pronoun because the dependents were in the high ground (al-akam), which lay between the Banu Qurayzah and those in the trench, so they were above the dependents and the men.

Since the intended sense of "above" was elevation of the land, He clarified it by saying: ﴿and from below you﴾, rather than saying "below you." This also conveys that those below only surrounded part of the men's side [only]. He did not say "from beneath you," lest it be thought that they were above the heads and beneath the feet. In the first clause He did not say "from higher than you," lest it contain a description of the disbelievers as exalted. The lower part of the land is the city from the direction of the west, meaning Quraysh and those of Kinanah who bordered them, since their route was from that side.

When He reminded them of the coming, which is the cause of fear, He reminded them of the fear by mentioning its time too, glorifying the matter by conjunction, saying: ﴿and when﴾, i.e., remember when. He made the verb and what is conjoined to it feminine, because the sense of the masculine, which revolves around strength, height and firmness, contradicts deviation. So He said: ﴿the eyes swerved﴾, i.e., turned away from the straightness of aim, like the act of one bewildered and distraught, because of the heedlessness arising from the astonishment produced by terror. He detached this from the attachment to the kaf of address out of consideration for them and to teach courtesy in address. Likewise: ﴿and the hearts reached the throats﴾, as a metaphor for the severity of terror and palpitation. It is also permissible, and this is the closer view, that this is literal: the spleen and the lungs are drawn upward to the top of the chest by their swelling at that moment. From this is the saying about the coward: "his nostril swelled," i.e., his lung. ﴿the throats﴾ is the plural of hanjarah, which is the end of the windpipe (al-hulqum). From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ, as narrated by Ahmad and Abu Dawud from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him): "The worst thing in a person is a cowardice that dislodges [the heart]," i.e., it pulls the heart out of its place. The plural of multiplicity indicates that this affected them all, or nearly all.

Since this was a state that arose, and then its outcome was either that it ceased and they remained steady until the matter ended, He expressed it in the past tense for that reason and to affirm it. And since from it arose the turning of hearts and the constant passing of thoughts in every direction, He expressed it in the present tense, which indicates the continuity of renewal, saying: ﴿and you were thinking about Allah﴾, who possesses the attributes of perfection, so no deficiency touches the sanctuary of His greatness, and no blemish approaches the side of His might, ﴿the thoughts﴾, i.e., what kinds of thinking. As for their variation among persons, it is clear, and it corresponds to the strength and weakness of faith. As for the single person, it varies according to changing circumstances: at times one thinks of destruction because of weakness, and at times of deliverance because Allah is capable of it. The hypocrites and those close to them among the weak of heart think what Allah related about them. Al-Razi said in al-Lawami': it is related that the Muslims said: "The hearts have reached the throats; is there anything we can say?" Then the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

"O Allah, conceal our faults and secure our frights."

The addition of the alif in the recitation of those who wrote it in both states, namely the two Madinan readers, Ibn 'Amir and Shu'bah, indicates the breadth of these thoughts and the diversity of those impulses. According to those who wrote it in pausal position but not in connected reading, namely Ibn Kathir, al-Kisa'i and Hafs, it indicates the variation of the state, at times with strength and at times with weakness.

Since severity in reality applies only to the steadfast, for he has nothing before him but destruction or victory, whereas the hypocrite offers peace and humiliation enters his home through agreeing to everything that is demanded of him, the commentator expressed the state of the believers by restricting the address to the leader (al-ra's), so that it would not enter into the content of the report. This signals that his noble station is too exalted to be tested. Thus the Exalted said: ﴿There﴾, i.e., at [that] great time, far-reaching in rank, ﴿the believers were tried﴾, i.e., those firmly rooted in faith were mixed with that which by its nature transforms what it mixes with and inclines it. He built the verb in the passive form because the intended purpose is only to know the sincere from others, along with the knowledge that the doer of that is the One to whom all command belongs. He did not emphasize the testing with the word for severity because the ifti'al pattern (the eighth verbal form, with its sense of effortful undergoing) already indicates it. The discourse was turned away from the address, along with the benefits mentioned earlier, and he expressed it by description in order to single out the firmly rooted, so he said: ﴿and they were shaken﴾, i.e., they were moved, pushed, disturbed, and unsettled by what they saw of terrors, through the united enmity of the foes despite their great number, and the spreading of rumors, ﴿with a severe shaking﴾. So they stood firm (p-304) by Allah's making them firm in their covenant.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 33, verse 12:

When it became known from this that the state that shook them was at the utmost of terror, he indicated that he had not shaken them by relating the sayings of those who were shaken, and he did not mention their sayings, though he will mention them later, so that the praise of them for steadfastness in the face of the great quaking would be mentioned twice, by indication and by explicit statement. So he said: ﴿And when﴾. He indicated their repetition of the sign of hypocrisy by using the present tense, so he said: ﴿say﴾, meaning again and again, ﴿the hypocrites﴾, meaning those firmly rooted in hypocrisy, because their hearts are diseased, full of sickness, ﴿and those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, meaning of the diseases of belief, to such a degree that it weakened them in belief and in steadfastness in the places of encounter and in every noble matter. They are such that they have not reached certainty in hypocrisy nor sincerity in faith, but are on an edge, so they have a kind of hypocrisy. The verse is an instance of ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which two complementary elements are each left implicit in one half and stated in the other): the mention of hypocrisy first indicates it second, and the mention of disease second indicates it first. [This which I have said about the hearts agrees with what the Imam al-Suhrawardi mentioned in the fifty-sixth chapter of his ʿAwarif from Hudhayfa, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Hearts are of four kinds: a bare heart in which there is a lamp shining, and that is the heart of the believer; a black, upturned heart, and that is the heart of the disbeliever; a heart tied up in a sheath, and that is the heart of the hypocrite; and a heart with two sides, in which there is both faith and hypocrisy. The likeness of faith in it is like the likeness of a herb that is nourished by good water (p-305), and the likeness of hypocrisy in it is like the likeness of a sore that is fed by pus and matter. Whichever of the two supplies predominates over it, it is judged by it." This hadith was also related by al-Ghazali at the end of the Book of the Foundations of Beliefs from his Ihya' from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, and Shaykh Zayn al-Din al-Iraqi said: "Ahmad recorded it."]

Since those who denied the promise of Allah, and to Allah be praise, were many, they emphasized their statement and mentioned the Greatest Name [and] attributed the Messenger to Him, so they said: ﴿What Allah promised us﴾, He who mentioned [to us] that He is encompassing of majesty and beauty, ﴿and His Messenger﴾, meaning the one of whom some among our people said that he is a messenger, mocking them, and establishing, in their claim, evidence for this affliction against the falsity of that claim, ﴿but delusion﴾, meaning falsehood by which he lured us away from what we were upon of our fathers' religion, and toward steadfastness in what we came to after that departure, by what he promised us of the victory of [this religion over] all religion and of establishment in the lands, even in the digging of the trench. For he said that he saw, through what gleamed for him when he struck the rock of Salman, the city of San'a in Yemen, the palaces of Kisra at al-Hira in the land of Persia, and the palaces of Syria in the land of the Romans, and that his followers would prevail over all of that. Allah has indeed fulfilled His promise in all of that, even in the case of Suraqa ibn Malik ibn Ju'shum wearing the bracelets of Kisra ibn Hurmuz, as is mentioned in full in al-Bayhaqi's Dala'il al-Nubuwwah. And they lied in their doubt.

So those who affirmed were triumphant, and those who were in their doubt, wavering, were lost.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 33, verse 13:

When He mentioned what is fundamental in their hypocrisy, which is denial (al-takdhib), He followed it with what branches out from it. Since their discouraging of others happened once through repetition, He expressed it in the past tense, saying: ﴿And when a group of them said﴾. He made the verb feminine, indicating their softness and effeminacy in their statements and actions. ﴿A group of them﴾ means a large number of those whose hearts are dead or diseased, circulating among one another, saying: ﴿O people of Yathrib﴾. They turned away from the name that the Prophet ﷺ had given the city, al-Madinah and Taybah, despite its goodness, to the name by which it was called in the past, even though that name could be disparaged, being derived from al-tharb (blame and reproach). This was to show their apostasy from Islam. In al-Jam' bayna al-'Ubab wa al-Muhkam (a combined work of al-'Ubab and al-Muhkam) he said: "Tharaba 'alayhi tharban wa atharba," with the meaning of tharraba tatriban, meaning he blamed him, reproached him for his sin, and reminded him of it.

They emphasized with the negation of the genus, because of how much they opposed this, and so they said: ﴿There is no place to stand for you﴾, meaning there is no standing, or no place of standing where you can stand. This is according to the reading of the majority with a fatha (maqam), and according to the reading of Hafs with a damma (muqam), meaning: there is no residing, or no place of residing, in the place of fighting and the clash of champions. ﴿So return﴾ to your homes in flight, and remain (p-307) with your women [as tails], or return to your former religion openly, so that you may have a hand (yad) with these armies.

When He mentioned those who tore away the veil and revealed the baseness of their condition, He followed them with others who concealed themselves somewhat, clinging to the skirts of hypocrisy out of fear of the terrors of dissension. He said: ﴿And a party of them seeks permission﴾, meaning they renew the request for permission at every moment, to return to their homes and to remain with the women. ﴿Of them, a party﴾, meaning a group whose nature is division, ask permission of ﴿the Prophet﴾, although they had seen what he possessed of lofty rank through his good character and form, and his noble qualities and dignified traits. They did not fear that we would inform him of their news or disclose to him what was hidden of the secrets of hearts and concealed matters, while they are ﴿saying﴾ [meaning] at every moment, emphatically, knowing their own lie and the believers' denial of them, their statement: ﴿Indeed, our houses are exposed﴾. They used the plural of abundance, indicating the large number of their hypocrite companions. ﴿Exposed﴾ means there is much weakness in them through which those of the factions who wish may enter. So if we go to them, we protect them from them and suffice against those among their corrupters who come to us, as a protection for the religion and a defense of the family.

When they said this, emphasizing it to him, Allah the Exalted refuted it, emphasizing His refutation and clarifying what they intended. He said: ﴿And they were not﴾, meaning and the situation is that they were not, [at that time in which they said this, and He emphasized the negation, saying:] ﴿exposed﴾, and they did not intend [by their going to protect them. ﴿Indeed﴾, meaning they did not intend] by their seeking permission ﴿except flight﴾.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 33, verse 14:

When their concern [was intense] with staying in their homes, they falsely displayed intense concern for guarding them, so God made that clear and indicated it by attributing it to the homes, [as an alert] that the homes are the lord of protection and the mainstay. So He said: ﴿And if it had been entered﴾, i.e., their houses, from any entrance whatsoever, by these confederates or others. He used the feminine form of the verb explicitly to indicate the intended meaning, and as an indication that what is attributed to them is deserving of weakness. He expressed it with the particle of elevation, saying: ﴿upon them﴾, indicating that it is an entry of dominance, ﴿from every side﴾, i.e., from all its sides, such that there would be no place for them to flee.

Since the intention of fleeing, along with encirclement of the dwelling from all sides, without striving to repel the attack in defense of family and property, far from the deeds of men, was [the case], He expressed it with the particle of delay, saying: ﴿Then they were asked﴾, i.e., by whatever questioner [was there], ﴿to commit sedition﴾, i.e., to come out of it, fleeing. It was as if He named it sedition because, since it was the gravest of sedition in that a person is not driven out of his house except by death or something close to it, it was as if there were no sedition other than it. ﴿They would have given it﴾, i.e., they would have committed sedition by coming out in flight, in response to the one who asked them, while strongly presuming that entry in the manner of encirclement meant there was no escape. So they always rely on fleeing without fighting, to protect their honor or to avert shame, or to defend a family or a neighbor. This meaning encompasses the reading of the people of the Hijaz with shortening (ʾātawhā), and others with lengthening (ʾāttawhā), for whoever agreed to flee has given what was as if in his hand of [steadfastness], out of cowardice, and has come to it and done it.

Since this was, among the Arabs, along with their courage and their fear of disgrace, hardly to be believed, He emphasized it to increase its depiction, saying: ﴿And they would not have delayed in them﴾, [i.e.] the houses, ﴿except briefly﴾. Thereby it is established that they intend only to flee, not to guard the houses from harm. What indicates this meaning is that He followed it, emphasizing, on account of their denial and their swearing falsely, with His saying:

(p. 310) ﴿Indeed they had already covenanted with God﴾, that is, these people who hastened to flee when they were confronted in that condition, with their women taken captive and their community destroyed, had covenanted with God, the One above whom there is no greater.

Since a covenant may be forgotten when much time has passed, which would be an excuse for the one who made it, he explained how recent the covenant was, after stating the greatness of the One with whom it was made and whose mention is therefore binding. So he said, affirming the preposition: ﴿from before﴾, that is, before this state and this expedition, when the true promises of conquests, which they now call deception, pleased them, at the time when the matter became serious and the conditions of jihad on which those conquests depended were required. ﴿They would not turn their backs﴾, that is, they would not approach their enemy and turn their backs ﴿ever﴾, for anything at all, and they would have no way of acting when the fury of battle grows hot, when people mix together, when the eyes turn red, when the men press against each other, and the brave defenders embrace one another, until victory or death.

Since a person may be lax about a covenant when the one who made it turns away from it, he said: ﴿And the covenant of God was ever to be questioned﴾, that is, the fulfilment of the covenant of Him who encompasses all attributes of perfection. Since the covenant is a supplementary element in speech, being an object, and since care for it is intensified here, he made this clear first by placing it at the beginning, then by making it the principal element, and secondly by attributing the verb to it, so he said: ﴿was ever to be questioned﴾, that is, as to whether the one who made it would fulfil it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 33, verse 16:

When Allah, glorified is He, had completed what He had informed His Messenger (ﷺ) of, as the expression "the Prophet" indicates, He resumed the matter by answering them, as an answer to one who seems to ask: "What is to be said to them?" and as a way of carrying the counsel on his tongue, because of the compassion with which he is naturally disposed. ﴿Say﴾, that is, to them, and He emphasized (the answer) because they supposed that fleeing would benefit them: ﴿It will not benefit you﴾, that is, in postponing your appointed terms at any time, ﴿the fleeing﴾, that is, the very fleeing for which your seeking leave was only on account of, ﴿if you flee from death﴾, that is, without an enemy, ﴿or killing﴾, because if the appointed term has [already] arrived, it will not be delayed by fleeing, and otherwise steadfastness will not shorten it. This is as ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say: "When the matter comes upon one suddenly, and the embers blaze, and the heat of war intensifies, on which of my two days do I flee from death? On the day not decreed, or the day decreed?" And this is because the term Allah has set is encompassing the human being, and he cannot at all exceed it. ﴿And then﴾, that is, and when you have fled.

Since they did not aim in living except at enjoyment, He clarified this with the passive form, saying: ﴿You will not be given enjoyment﴾, that is, enjoyment that is extended as you desire with what remains of your lives, if any of them remains, ﴿except for a little﴾. Rather, the enemy will overpower you from your backs, and from your wealth, your honor, and your homes, and will corrupt whatever he is able to of that, and you will not be able to repair it except after a long time and great toil. This is in contrast to what happens if you stand firm, fulfilling the covenant and preserving good repute, and meet the opponents and clash with the horsemen, relying upon your Lord and obeying your Prophet. Then, if the term has come, that will not diminish anything for you, and you will die honored and noble; and otherwise, you will attain victory, gain the reward, and live in the most complete blessing until the end of your lives. So steadfastness is more lasting for the souls and more preserving of the joyful life.

(p-312) Since they are bound by illusion and turn with the senses, as beasts do, they were bound to say: "Yes, it will benefit us, for we have often seen that whoever fled was safe, and whoever stood firm was uprooted." So He commanded him to answer this with His words: ﴿Say﴾, that is, to them, rebuking them: ﴿Who is it that can protect you﴾, that is, prevent you, ﴿from Allah﴾, who encompasses everything in power and knowledge, before the flight, during it, and after it, ﴿if He intends for you harm﴾, so that He sends His vengeance upon you, and then none can repel that harm from you; ﴿or﴾ He humiliates you, disgraces your side, and degrades it by afflicting you with evil, ﴿if He intends for you mercy﴾, so that He grants you His bounties. Mercy means benefit, and it is named so because it is its effect. Measure this meaning by the standards of your intellects, reasoning from what you have found of the two sides throughout your lives. Did you guard yourselves against an evil intention, and did that guarding benefit you? Did someone other than Him strive to prevent a mercy from Him, and his purpose was accomplished? Or did Allah bring upon you something of that, and did anyone, despite exerting effort, manage to lift it without His permission? It is possible that the verse is an instance of ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which each of two opposites is mentioned in one place and omitted in another, the omitted one being implied by its counterpart): He mentioned harm first as an indication of the omission of its opposite second, and He mentioned mercy second as an indication of the omission of its opposite first.

Since they were the most obstinate of people, Allah, glorified is He, indicated, by their not hastening to answer with what would point to the reply against their obstinacy, through the conjunction with what is known to be its implied answer from every discerning person: no one besides Him can protect them from any of that, nor can anyone afflict them with any of it. So He said: ﴿And they will not find﴾, that is, at any time, ﴿for themselves﴾. He drew attention to the fact that there is nothing except that it is in His grip, glorified is He, and that nothing else has any power to encompass anything, not even the ranks beneath His rank, by His words, affirming the preposition: ﴿besides Allah﴾. He expressed it with the proper name to indicate His encompassing of every beautiful attribute. How, then, could anything other than Him have any share in any of them except by His permission? ﴿a protector﴾, who would befriend them and benefit them in some kind of benefit, ﴿nor a helper﴾, who would support them against His command, so as to turn back from them whatever evil He intended.

When He, glorified is He, informed them of what He knew of the secrets they had concealed, and commanded him (ﷺ) to admonish them, He warned them that His knowledge is constant regarding whoever among them betrays. So He said, confirming and bringing near the past tense and indicating that this attribute continues for Him: ﴿Allah certainly knows﴾. Perhaps He used "qad" (certainly), which may in this construction convey the sense of paucity, to indicate that for one who has even a minimal degree of intellect, it suffices to fear the might of the one who threatens, the possibility of His knowing. He expressed it with the Greatest Name (al-Ism al-A'zam), the Name that comprises all divine attributes, saying ﴿Allah﴾, to indicate that majesty and beauty encompass all. ﴿The hinderers﴾, that is, those who discourage others with discouragement that is hateful and disobedient, hastening toward it as one who is seized hastens, not by his own choice. ﴿From among you﴾, that is, you who have professed faith before people in general, ﴿who keep others back from coming to the presence of the Messenger (ﷺ)﴾. ﴿And those who say to their brothers, "Come here to us"﴾, that is, come and approach, ﴿to us,﴾ giving the impression that their side is one where fighting takes place and where righteous deeds are constantly practiced. ﴿And they do not﴾, that is, while the state is that they do not ﴿come to battle﴾, that is, to war or its place, ﴿except a little﴾, for show and reputation, to the extent that the sincere ones see them. So when they become occupied with the fighting, and each one is preoccupied with what concerns him, they slip away from them, sheltering themselves with one who cannot benefit them from among the creatures, seeking refuge.

[p. 315] When they gave each of these actions a fitting justification, he exposed the corruption of their intent by saying, condemning them in the strongest terms through the expression *al-shuhh* (stinginess, which is extreme niggardliness). It is stinginess with what is in one's hand, and it is also a command to the unseen to be stingy, so it is stinginess upon stinginess: an evil, filthy stinginess, persisted in and hastened toward. ﴿Stingy towards you﴾ means that they do these things while each of them is grudging toward you, with regard to the benefit of any gain from them or from others, whether of self or of wealth.

Since the presumed context was a state of security, he followed it with a description of their state in fear, saying: ﴿And when fear comes﴾, meaning, because its causes have come, namely war and its preliminaries, ﴿you see them﴾, meaning, O addressee, ﴿looking at you﴾. He indicated their remoteness physically and figuratively by the particle of limit, saying: ﴿towards you﴾, meaning while they are ﴿turning﴾ right and left, ﴿their eyes rolling﴾ by the movement of the glance, meaning, swerving out of terror and cowardice. Then he likened the rapidity of their rolling, which lacks any sound purpose, saying: ﴿like one who﴾, meaning like the rolling of the eye of one who, and he showed the intensity of concern by portraying this through making the object the principal element with the verb built for it, saying: ﴿is overcome with faintness﴾, beginning his loss of consciousness, ﴿from death﴾. This is the way of God in that everyone who deals with people by deceit is weak in steadfastness at the clash of arms.

Then he mentioned another particular feature to show their cowardice, saying: ﴿But when fear departs﴾, meaning with the departure of its causes, ﴿they assail you﴾, meaning they attack you with harsh assault, out of boldness and impudence, forgetting what has recently occurred from them of cowardice and weakness, ﴿with sharp tongues﴾, cutting, piercing, eloquent, after they were, in the time of fear, in the utmost stammering, unable to move because of the scarcity of saliva and the dryness of the lips. This is for the sake of the perishable worldly goods of the spoils or other things. Then he explained the meaning of his saying ﴿stingy﴾, meaning, stingy in an overbearing manner ﴿towards the good﴾, meaning the wealth they possess, and in their belief that there is no good other than it, stingy in a way that they do not want any of it to reach you and nothing of it to escape them. This is another practice of God: whoever is firm in ease is slack in hardship and at the time of encounter. I have interpreted *al-shuhh* in this way because its root, in its arrangement, revolves around gathering that has reached corruption, from *al-hashish* (dry herbage) and *al-mihashsha* (the anus). Thus it is a gathering that is usually followed by distress and harm. Among the necessary consequences of gathering in general is strength, which is followed by hardness, and sometimes harshness arises from it, and sometimes division arises from gathering, which entails softness. So from distressful gathering comes *shuhh*, which is stinginess and greed, and *shuhh al-nafs* is the soul's greed for what it possesses. Al-Qazzaz said: the plural of *shahih* in the smallest number is *ashihha*, and I have not heard other than this. Abu Yusuf related: *ashiha'* (with the long vowel, in the plural of many). And "the two men *yatashahhan*" concerning a matter when each of them wants not to miss it. A *zand shahhah* is a firestick that does not kindle. *Ma' shahhah* is distressful water, not abundant, because its gathering has become intense in its place and its ground has become firm through the gathering of its parts, so it became very hard and withheld itself. *Ard shahhah* means hard ground. Al-Qazzaz said: the firestick was likened to it. *Al-shahshah* is the sharp, the bad-tempered, the forward in speech or movement, and the one persistent in something, because these are necessary consequences of sharpness arising from strength that arises from gathering. From here the eloquent orator, the brave man, and the zealous are called *shahshah* and *shahshah*. *Al-shahshah* among crows is the one with much voice; among donkeys, the light one; among sand grouse, the swift one. *Al-shahshah* is the tall one, as if he gathered two heights. The camel *shahshaha* in its roaring when it does not free it, as if it gathered to the roaring what is not roaring. *Al-shahshaha* is the sound of the sand grouse because of its continuous connection, so it returns to the sharpness that returns to the strength arising from gathering. Also the repetition of the camel's roaring, rapid flight, and caution, for it indicates collectedness of heart and sharpness of mind. A *mar'a shahshah* is as if she were a man in her strength. *Al-mushahshah*, like *al-musalsal*, is the one of little good. *Ibil shahaih* are camels of little milk, and this is from gathering and hardness arising from harshness and distress. *Al-shahih* of the land is what flows from the least rain, because of its hardness and the intensity of the gathering of some of it to some others. *Al-shahshah* also refers to land that does not flow except from much rain, the opposite of the first, and this looks to its gathering for seeing into its depth, because in its parts there is the division mentioned earlier as a necessary consequence of gathering. From gathering in general comes the wide wasteland, because it gathers what is to be gathered. *Al-shihab* are small valleys that drive water into the wadi, so by their extension they are gathering, and by their being small they are distressful and gathered in themselves. From gathering comes *al-hashish*, which is dry herbage, and its origin is what has been gathered from it.

*Al-mihashsh* is the place abundant in herbage and goodness, because gathering may arise from it as kindness, and abundance of herbage entails kindness in feeding the animals, and its land will be good. One who *hashsha al-hashish* cuts it. *Fulan* means he improved his condition. *Al-mal* means he multiplied it. *Zaydan ba'iran aw bi-ba'irin* means he gave him a camel. *Al-hashsh* (with a fatha) is the exit. *Al-mihashsha* is the anus. *Al-hashsh* is the garden with gathered palm trees. The privy was named after it because the Arabs used to relieve themselves there. *Hashsh Talha* and *Hashsh Kawkab* are two places in Madina. *Hashsha al-walad fi al-batn* means the fetus dried up. A woman *ahashshat* and so is *mihashsh*, when the fetus has dried up within her womb. *Al-hushsh* (with a damma) is the dead fetus in the womb. *Hashashtu al-faras* means I gathered herbage for it. *Ahashshtu al-rajul* means I helped him to gather herbage. *Al-hishash* is the sack that contains herbage. *Ahashsha al-kala'* means the pasture became possible to be mown. *Al-mustahasha* from the she-camels is one whose lower legs have become slender, meaning from the part above her pastern to her shank, and this is due to its largeness and abundance of fat. *Istahasha al-ghusn* means the branch grew long, as if it gathered two lengths, or became such that it gathers much foliage, one thing with another. *Hashsha al-widiyya* from the palm means it dried up. From gathering: *hashsha al-sayd* means he gathered the game from its two sides, and *al-faras* means he threw herbage to the horse. Al-Qazzaz said: this is the dryness of the pasture, and its origin is what is gathered. From it: "I mow for you and you dung for me," said of one who does evil to one who has done good to him.
